# Reflex

> GGUF-native GPU inference engine optimized for cold-start latency and energy (process
> launch to first token), not sustained server throughput. Every CUDA kernel is compiled
> ahead-of-time by `nvcc` at build time (`build.rs`) — never at runtime via NVRTC — so
> there is no JIT tax on cold start. `batch_size` is always 1; no in-engine HTTP server,
> queue, or continuous batching (see "Non-goals" in README.md). Full context: README.md,
> docs/reference.md, docs/benchmarks.md, docs/DEVELOPMENT.md, CHANGELOG.md.

This file gives an agent the literal commands to run Reflex on each supported platform.
Every command below is real and has been executed against real GPU hardware at least
once — see each platform's linked README for the measured numbers and any caveats.

## Prerequisites, all platforms

A GGUF model file. The project's own benchmarks/fixtures center on `Qwen3-0.6B-Q4_K_M`
(~379MB) — e.g. `unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF` on Hugging Face. Reflex auto-detects dense,
MoE, hybrid (Qwen3.5 Gated DeltaNet), MLA (DeepSeek-V2/V3) and Kolibri-1 architectures from
GGUF metadata; no flag needed (Kolibri-1's 78B `Q4_K_M` also needs
`REFLEX_QUANT_RESIDENT=1` to fit on one GPU).

An NVIDIA GPU with a known compute capability, since a from-source build defaults to
portable PTX (small driver-JIT cost) unless you pin `REFLEX_CUDA_ARCH=sm_XX` for a true
zero-JIT cubin build. Common values: `sm_75` (T4, most AWS/some Runpod GPUs), `sm_86`
(A4500/A6000/3090-class, Runpod's cheapest serverless pool), `sm_89` (L4/Ada, Modal's
`gpu="L4"`). **A pinned cubin only runs on the exact compute capability it was built
for** — this is the single most common mistake across every platform below.

## Local GPU

Requires the CUDA toolkit (`nvcc` on `PATH` or `CUDA_PATH`/`CUDA_HOME`).

```
cargo build --release
cargo run --release --bin reflex -- smoke                          # proves the AOT pipeline works end to end
cargo run --release --bin reflex -- generate <path-to-gguf> "prompt"
```

`REFLEX_CUDA_ARCH=sm_86 cargo build --release` pins a cubin to one GPU instead of
portable PTX. `REFLEX_SKIP_CUDA=1 cargo build` skips kernel compilation for editing on a
machine with no CUDA toolkit (no subcommand actually runs on this build). Run `reflex` with no
arguments for the subcommand list (`system1`, `bench`, `check`, `stdio`/`uds` IPC modes,
etc.) and `reflex <subcommand>` for its usage; `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` covers building and testing.

## Docker (any host with `nvidia-container-toolkit`)

```
docker build -t reflex .   # multi-arch fatbin; --build-arg REFLEX_CUDA_ARCH=sm_XX pins one GPU arch
docker run --rm --gpus all -v /path/to/models:/models \
  reflex /models/Qwen3-0.6B-Q4_K_M.gguf "Once upon a time"
```

Default entrypoint is `reflex generate`. For any other subcommand, override it:
`docker run --rm --gpus all -v /path/to/models:/models --entrypoint /usr/local/bin/reflex reflex smoke`.

## AWS

**Fastest path — one GPU instance, no autoscaling**: launch a `g4dn.xlarge` (Tesla T4,
`sm_75`) from a DLAMI with Docker + NVIDIA Container Toolkit preinstalled
(`base-oss-nvidia-driver-gpu-ubuntu-22.04`, resolved via
`aws ssm get-parameter --name /aws/service/deeplearning/ami/x86_64/base-oss-nvidia-driver-gpu-ubuntu-22.04/latest/ami-id`),
ship this repo to it, then run the Docker recipe above with `REFLEX_CUDA_ARCH=sm_75`. No
SSH key needed — use SSM Session Manager (`AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` on the
instance's IAM role) for shell access.

**Production pattern (Spot GPU instances, Auto Scaling Group, scale-to-zero, EFS shared
model cache, `reflex uds` sidecar over a local Unix Domain Socket)**: see
[`docs/aws-deployment.md`](docs/aws-deployment.md). **Always-warm alternative** (On-Demand
instance, public HTTPS load balancer, `sidecar/openai-adapter` HTTP sidecar instead of
raw UDS): see [`docs/aws-deployment-warm.md`](docs/aws-deployment-warm.md).

## Runpod

**Recommended: [`serverless/runpod/`](serverless/runpod/README.md)** — a Runpod
Serverless **Load-Balancing** endpoint (not queue-based; the existing
`reflex-openai-adapter` HTTP sidecar runs unmodified, zero Python glue).
[`scripts/deploy_runpod.sh`](scripts/deploy_runpod.sh) automates the whole path: it builds
and pushes the image, creates the load-balancing template + endpoint, pins the `sm_86`
SKU, and runs the cold-start benchmark (`scripts/bench_cold_runpod.sh`) against it.
The image uses the slim `base` + `libcublas-12-4` runtime and multi-arch fatbin kernels by
default (see the README's image-size section). To do it by hand, build and push the root
`Dockerfile`'s `runpod-lb` target (`docker build --target runpod-lb .`), then create the endpoint (console, API,
or `runpod-mcp`'s `create-endpoint` / `runpodctl`) with:
- Endpoint type: Load Balancing
- `GGUF_PATH` env var (model is baked into the image at build time), `PORT` if not `80`
- **Pin the GPU SKU to RTX A4500** (`sm_86`) only for a single-arch image
  (`REFLEX_CUDA_ARCH=sm_86`) or a benchmark: the cheapest pool `AMPERE_16` is
  mixed-architecture (also contains Ada `sm_89` cards) despite its name. The default
  multi-arch fatbin image runs natively on every card in it (verified on an A4500 and an
  L4, 2026-10-02).
- Do not rely on `HEALTH_CHECK_PATH` — Runpod's gateway polls the hardcoded `/ping` path
  regardless; the adapter serves the same three-state health check at both paths.

Real measured result: ~3.4x faster cold start than Runpod's own official `worker-vllm`
on identical hardware — see [`docs/serverless-cost-comparison.md`](docs/serverless-cost-comparison.md).

**Runpod Hub listing** (browsable catalog, one-click deploy):
<https://console.runpod.io/hub/lateos-ai/reflex>, built from [`.runpod/`](.runpod/README.md)
— a second, parallel, queue-based build required only because the Hub's publishing pipeline
doesn't currently accept load-balancing endpoints. Deploy from that page, or with
`runpod-mcp`'s `deploy-hub-repo` / `runpodctl hub` for `lateos-ai/reflex`. Job `input` is an
OpenAI chat-completions body; `"stream": true` streams chunks via `/stream/{job_id}`, and a
non-streaming job's `output` is a one-element list holding the `chat.completion`. The
optional `ADAPTER_ARGS` env var passes extra `reflex-openai-adapter` flags (request limits
etc.). Prefer `serverless/runpod/` for a manual/direct deployment.

## Modal

```
PYTHONUTF8=1 python -m modal run .modal/app.py       # one-shot: ephemeral App, real cold-start measurement, tears down after
PYTHONUTF8=1 python -m modal deploy .modal/app.py    # persistent deployment
```

`PYTHONUTF8=1` works around a Windows console encoding crash on Modal's CLI Unicode
output — omit it on Linux/macOS. Builds from `.modal/Dockerfile` (same builder recipe as
`serverless/runpod/`, `REFLEX_CUDA_ARCH=sm_89` for Modal's `gpu="L4"`), model baked in.
See [`.modal/README.md`](.modal/README.md) for real measured numbers (~7-8s cold start,
`n=3`) and [`docs/modal-phase3-comparison.md`](docs/modal-phase3-comparison.md) for a
controlled comparison against plain vLLM on the same platform (~25x faster).

## Non-goals, so an agent doesn't propose them

`batch_size` is always 1. No internal request queue/scheduler, no continuous batching,
no in-engine HTTP/gRPC server — ever. Multi-tenancy and any network-facing serving layer
belong in a host orchestrator or one of the sidecar/adapter binaries above, never inside
the core `reflex` engine. See README.md's "Non-goals" section for the full rationale
before proposing anything in this direction.
